RESCINDED JOB OFFER AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL (SHEPPARD V. MORGAN KEEGAN; TOSCANO V. GREENE MUSIC) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes what California law says when a job offer is withdrawn after the person who accepted it has already acted on it — most commonly by resigning from another job, or by relocating — but before the new employment begins. It draws on the at-will presumption in Labor Code section 2922; on the Court of Appeal's decision in Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan & Co. (1990) 218 Cal.App.3d 61, which reversed a summary judgment for an employer that "separated" a new hire before his first day after he had quit his prior job and leased an apartment across the country, and identified the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing and the doctrine of promissory estoppel as the governing principles; and on Toscano v. Greene Music (2004) 124 Cal.App.4th 685, which describes the elements of promissory estoppel, holds that a person who resigned from at-will employment in reliance on an unfulfilled promise of a new job may recover the wages lost from the former employer as reliance damages, and explains the reasonable-certainty proof standard that limits such an award. It also notes the Fair Employment and Housing Act provision (Government Code section 12940, subdivision (a)) that makes refusing to hire a person because of a protected characteristic an unlawful employment practice. Where a specific employer and jobseeker are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference. This sheet is a companion to this corpus's information sheets on fraudulent inducement of employment (the promissory-fraud claim under Lazar v. Superior Court, which requires a promise made without intent to perform), on Labor Code sections 970 through 972 (the statutory remedy for inducing a change of residence through knowingly false representations), and on the at-will presumption and implied-in-fact contract limits under Guz v. Bechtel; it does not restate those materials. The doctrine described here is different from fraud: promissory estoppel does not require proof that the employer never intended to honor the offer, only that a clear promise was made, was reasonably and foreseeably relied on, and caused a substantial detriment.

THE AT-WILL PRESUMPTION AND WHY IT APPLIES TO AN OFFER THAT HAS NOT YET STARTED (LABOR CODE SECTION 2922)
Labor Code section 2922 provides that an employment having no specified term may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other, and that employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month. In Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan & Co., the Court of Appeal described this section as establishing a presumption that, in the absence of an express oral or written agreement specifying the length of employment or the grounds for termination, the employment is at will, and stated that the presumption may be overcome by evidence that the parties agreed, despite the absence of a specified term, that the employer's power to terminate would be limited in some way — for example, that termination would be permitted only for good cause. The court applied the presumption to an offer that had been accepted but not yet begun: the offer in that case was for an indefinite term, the acceptance did not include an agreement to work for a specified period, and the court found that a recruiting statement about salary, a guaranteed minimum bonus, and expected first-year earnings was not the kind of communication from an employer that indicates assurance of ongoing employment absent good cause for termination. Toscano v. Greene Music likewise treated the promised position as at-will employment, quoting the California Supreme Court's statement in Guz v. Bechtel that an at-will employment may be ended by either party at any time without cause, for any or no reason, and subject to no procedure except the statutory requirement of notice. As the following clauses describe, both courts nonetheless recognized that the at-will character of the promised job does not by itself end the inquiry when the offer is withdrawn after the applicant has relied on it.

THE DOCTRINE OF PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AND ITS ELEMENTS (TOSCANO V. GREENE MUSIC; SHEPPARD V. MORGAN KEEGAN)
Promissory estoppel is the doctrine California courts have applied when a job offer is withdrawn after the applicant has relied on it. In Toscano v. Greene Music, the Court of Appeal, quoting the California Supreme Court's decision in Kajima/Ray Wilson v. Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority, stated the doctrine in the words of section 90 of the Restatement Second of Contracts: a promise which the promisor should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee or a third person, and which does induce such action or forbearance, is binding if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement of the promise, and the remedy granted for breach may be limited as justice requires. The court explained that promissory estoppel is a doctrine which employs equitable principles to satisfy the requirement that consideration must be given in exchange for the promise sought to be enforced — that is, the promisee's reliance substitutes for the consideration that an ordinary contract requires. Toscano lists the elements as (1) a clear promise, (2) reliance, (3) substantial detriment, and (4) damages measured by the extent of the obligation assumed and not performed. Fourteen years earlier, Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan & Co. had quoted the same Restatement formulation and stated that the employer's conduct in withdrawing an accepted offer before the start date is governed by the doctrine of promissory estoppel. In Toscano, the plaintiff had pleaded breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, promissory estoppel, and interference with prospective economic advantage; only the promissory estoppel claim survived summary adjudication, and the case went to a bench trial on that claim alone.

AN ACCEPTED OFFER WITHDRAWN BEFORE THE FIRST DAY, AFTER THE NEW HIRE HAS QUIT AND RELOCATED (SHEPPARD V. MORGAN KEEGAN & CO.)
Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan & Co. is the California decision most directly addressing an accepted job offer withdrawn before the start date. A Memphis investment banking firm recruited a California stock analyst, interviewed him in Memphis, and offered him a position for an indefinite term at a $60,000 base salary with an expected minimum bonus of $25,000. He accepted by telephone two weeks later and quit his California job the same day. He then flew to Memphis to obtain housing, set up his office, meet his secretary, fill out insurance forms, and order business cards; leased an apartment; and returned to California to pack. Before he began working, the firm's managing director informed him by telephone that the firm had decided to "separate" him, and, when asked why, said he did not know. The firm reimbursed the two trips to Memphis but not the apartment deposit or any salary. The trial court granted the firm summary judgment. The Court of Appeal reversed. It held that although the analyst had not shown that the firm needed good cause to terminate him, implicit in such an employment agreement — and certainly implicit within the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, which the court described as inherent in every contract — is the understanding that an employer cannot expect a new employee to sever his former employment and move across the country only to be terminated before the ink dries on his new lease, or before he has had a chance to demonstrate his ability to satisfy the requirements of the job. The court added that the employer's conduct was governed by promissory estoppel, and adopted the reasoning of the Minnesota Supreme Court in Grouse v. Group Health Plan, Inc., a case in which an offer was revoked before the plaintiff started work: under those facts the plaintiff had a right to assume he would be given a good-faith opportunity to perform his duties to the employer's satisfaction once he was on the job. Because the firm's stated reasons for the separation were either conclusory or disputed, the court held the question could not be resolved on summary judgment.

WHAT A PERSON WHO QUIT A JOB FOR A WITHDRAWN OFFER CAN RECOVER: RELIANCE DAMAGES MEASURED BY THE FORMER JOB (TOSCANO V. GREENE MUSIC)
Toscano v. Greene Music addresses the measure of damages when an offer is withdrawn after the applicant has resigned from other employment. The plaintiff, the general manager of a piano store, was offered a sales management position by another piano retailer to start on September 1, 2001; he resigned from his existing job on August 1 in reliance on that promise, and in mid-August the new employer withdrew the offer. He later found lower-paying work. After a bench trial on promissory estoppel, the trial court awarded him lost wages measured by what he would have earned from his former employer. On appeal, the plaintiff conceded that the weight of authority prevents an employee in his circumstances from recovering future lost wages from the prospective employer that induced him to resign — the wages of the job he never started — but argued that the law permits recovery of what he would have earned in the future from his former employer as a component of reliance damages. The Court of Appeal agreed with that framing. It noted the California Supreme Court's observation that, unless there is unjust enrichment of the promisor, promissory estoppel damages should not put the promisee in a better position than performance of the promise would have put him, but held that this limitation does not preclude recovery of some measure of future income relinquished as a result of detrimental reliance. Given the equitable underpinnings of the doctrine, the court held that a plaintiff who relinquished his job in reliance on an unfulfilled promise of employment may, on an appropriate showing, recover the lost wages he would have expected to earn from his former employer but for the defendant's promise. The court rejected the argument that the at-will nature of the former job is a strict impediment to such recovery, reasoning by analogy to the tort of interference with an at-will contract that an at-will relationship is at the will of the parties, not of outsiders, and that assessing such damages against the third-party promisor rather than against the at-will employer does not contradict or undermine California's doctrine of at-will employment.

THE LIMIT: LOST FUTURE WAGES FROM THE FORMER JOB MUST BE PROVEN WITH REASONABLE CERTAINTY (TOSCANO V. GREENE MUSIC)
Toscano's damages holding carries an express limit. The Court of Appeal stated at the outset that lost wages from the former employer are recoverable on a promissory estoppel theory as long as they are not speculative or remote and are supported by substantial evidence, and it applied what it called the settled rule that a damage award in these circumstances must not be speculative, remote, contingent, or merely possible. Analogizing to lost-profits claims, the court held that damages for the loss of future earnings in this context are recoverable where the evidence makes reasonably certain their occurrence and extent, and described the only limitation on the plaintiff's recovery as the requirement that the fact and extent of his lost future earnings be proven with reasonable certainty. On the record before it, the court found that standard unmet as to the award of wages from September 1, 2001 (the promised start date) through the plaintiff's projected retirement in 2017. The plaintiff's accountant had calculated the difference between his former salary and his new earnings through retirement, but admitted she was unaware of any specific tenure at the former job and that he could have quit or been fired at any time; her testimony did not establish that he had a definite expectation of continued employment with the former employer for any particular period, and the plaintiff's own history of staying with employers until offered new work did not establish with reasonable certainty that an at-will employer would have kept him until the end of his career. Although the fact of damage was established, the court held the expert's conclusions as to its extent were wholly conjectural. The defendant had conceded that the plaintiff was entitled to one month of salary from the former employer — from his August 1 resignation to the promised September 1 start date. The court vacated the award of future earnings from September 1, 2001 to retirement, remanded for a new trial limited to the amount of those damages, and otherwise affirmed the judgment.

WITHDRAWING AN OFFER FOR A REASON THE LAW PROHIBITS: FEHA'S REFUSAL-TO-HIRE PROVISION (GOVERNMENT CODE SECTION 12940, SUBDIVISION (A))
The promissory estoppel doctrine described in the preceding clauses does not depend on the employer's reason for withdrawing the offer. A separate body of law addresses the reason itself. Government Code section 12940 declares it an unlawful employment practice — unless based upon a bona fide occupational qualification, or except where based upon applicable security regulations established by the United States or the State of California — for an employer, because of a person's race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status, to refuse to hire or employ the person, or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment. The statute's operative verbs — refuse to hire or employ, bar, and discharge — describe employer decisions at every stage from application through separation, and the statute does not confine its coverage to persons who have already begun work. This corpus's separate information sheets on discriminatory job advertisements and applicant inquiries, on the Fair Chance Act, and on post-offer medical examinations describe other statutory limits on hiring-stage decisions.

HOW THIS DOCTRINE RELATES TO OTHER CLAIMS DESCRIBED IN THIS CORPUS
Three other information sheets in this corpus describe claims that can arise from the same facts as a withdrawn offer, and each has different requirements from the promissory estoppel doctrine summarized here. The sheet on fraudulent inducement of employment describes the tort of promissory fraud under Lazar v. Superior Court, which requires that the employer's promise have been made without any intention of performing it and which, if proven, opens the door to tort damages and, under Civil Code section 3294, exemplary damages; promissory estoppel, by contrast, requires no showing of dishonest intent at the time of the promise and yields reliance-based relief. The sheet on Labor Code sections 970 through 972 describes the statutory remedy — double damages and a misdemeanor — for inducing a person to change residence for work through knowingly false representations about the kind, character, existence, or duration of the work; it applies only where a change of residence was induced and only where the representations were knowingly false. The sheet on the at-will presumption and implied-in-fact contracts under Guz v. Bechtel describes the contract-based limits on terminating an employment that has already begun. Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan itself was pleaded as breach of contract, fraud, and wrongful termination, and Toscano v. Greene Music as breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant, promissory estoppel, and interference with prospective economic advantage; in Toscano only the promissory estoppel claim reached trial. Nothing in this sheet evaluates which, if any, of these theories fits a particular situation.

expectedJSON.body: This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes what California law says when a job offer is withdrawn after the person who accepted it has already acted on it — most commonly by resigning from another job, or by relocating — but before the new employment begins. It draws on the at-will presumption in Labor Code section 2922; on the Court of Appeal's decision in Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan & Co. (1990) 218 Cal.App.3d 61, which reversed a summary judgment for an employer that "separated" a new hire before his first day after he had quit his prior job and leased an apartment across the country, and identified the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing and the doctrine of promissory estoppel as the governing principles; and on Toscano v. Greene Music (2004) 124 Cal.App.4th 685, which describes the elements of promissory estoppel, holds that a person who resigned from at-will employment in reliance on an unfulfilled promise of a new job may recover the wages lost from the former employer as reliance damages, and explains the reasonable-certainty proof standard that limits such an award. It also notes the Fair Employment and Housing Act provision (Government Code section 12940, subdivision (a)) that makes refusing to hire a person because of a protected characteristic an unlawful employment practice. Where a specific employer and jobseeker are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference. This sheet is a companion to this corpus's information sheets on fraudulent inducement of employment (the promissory-fraud claim under Lazar v. Superior Court, which requires a promise made without intent to perform), on Labor Code sections 970 through 972 (the statutory remedy for inducing a change of residence through knowingly false representations), and on the at-will presumption and implied-in-fact contract limits under Guz v. Bechtel; it does not restate those materials. The doctrine described here is different from fraud: promissory estoppel does not require proof that the employer never intended to honor the offer, only that a clear promise was made, was reasonably and foreseeably relied on, and caused a substantial detriment.

Labor Code section 2922 provides that an employment having no specified term may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other, and that employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month. In Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan & Co., the Court of Appeal described this section as establishing a presumption that, in the absence of an express oral or written agreement specifying the length of employment or the grounds for termination, the employment is at will, and stated that the presumption may be overcome by evidence that the parties agreed, despite the absence of a specified term, that the employer's power to terminate would be limited in some way — for example, that termination would be permitted only for good cause. The court applied the presumption to an offer that had been accepted but not yet begun: the offer in that case was for an indefinite term, the acceptance did not include an agreement to work for a specified period, and the court found that a recruiting statement about salary, a guaranteed minimum bonus, and expected first-year earnings was not the kind of communication from an employer that indicates assurance of ongoing employment absent good cause for termination. Toscano v. Greene Music likewise treated the promised position as at-will employment, quoting the California Supreme Court's statement in Guz v. Bechtel that an at-will employment may be ended by either party at any time without cause, for any or no reason, and subject to no procedure except the statutory requirement of notice. As the following clauses describe, both courts nonetheless recognized that the at-will character of the promised job does not by itself end the inquiry when the offer is withdrawn after the applicant has relied on it.

citations.quote: An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. Employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month.
This section establishes a presumption that in the absence of an express oral or written agreement which specifies the length of employment or grounds for termination, the employment is at will.

The presumption of an at-will contract may be overcome by evidence that, despite the absence of a specified term, the parties agreed that the employer’s power to terminate would be limited in some way, for example, that termination would be permitted only for “good cause.”
The offer was for an indefinite term. At the time, appellant was employed in a similar position with a California company.
His acceptance did not include an agreement to work for a specified period of time.

Thus, the managing director’s statement to appellant that he would receive a $60,000 annual salary plus $25,000 guaranteed minimum bonus, and be earning between $110,000 and $120,000 within one year is not the kind of communication from an employer that indicates assurance of ongoing employment absent good cause for termination.
An at-will employment may be ended by either party ‘at any time without cause,’ for any or no reason, and subject to no procedure except the statutory requirement of notice.

expectedJSON.body: Promissory estoppel is the doctrine California courts have applied when a job offer is withdrawn after the applicant has relied on it. In Toscano v. Greene Music, the Court of Appeal, quoting the California Supreme Court's decision in Kajima/Ray Wilson v. Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority, stated the doctrine in the words of section 90 of the Restatement Second of Contracts: a promise which the promisor should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee or a third person, and which does induce such action or forbearance, is binding if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement of the promise, and the remedy granted for breach may be limited as justice requires. The court explained that promissory estoppel is a doctrine which employs equitable principles to satisfy the requirement that consideration must be given in exchange for the promise sought to be enforced — that is, the promisee's reliance substitutes for the consideration that an ordinary contract requires. Toscano lists the elements as (1) a clear promise, (2) reliance, (3) substantial detriment, and (4) damages measured by the extent of the obligation assumed and not performed. Fourteen years earlier, Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan & Co. had quoted the same Restatement formulation and stated that the employer's conduct in withdrawing an accepted offer before the start date is governed by the doctrine of promissory estoppel. In Toscano, the plaintiff had pleaded breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, promissory estoppel, and interference with prospective economic advantage; only the promissory estoppel claim survived summary adjudication, and the case went to a bench trial on that claim alone.

The remedy granted for breach may be limited as justice requires.’
Promissory estoppel is ‘a doctrine which employs equitable principles to satisfy the requirement that consideration must be given in exchange for the promise sought to be enforced.’
The elements of promissory estoppel are (1) a clear promise, (2) reliance, (3) substantial detriment, and (4) damages “measured by the extent of the obligation assumed and not performed.”

Further, the employer’s conduct here is governed by the doctrine of promissory estoppel, which provides: “A promise which the promisor should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee or a third person and which does induce such action or forbearance is binding if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement of the promise.”
Only his claim for promissory estoppel survived summary adjudication, and the matter proceeded to a bench trial.

expectedJSON.body: Sheppard v. Morgan Keegan & Co. is the California decision most directly addressing an accepted job offer withdrawn before the start date. A Memphis investment banking firm recruited a California stock analyst, interviewed him in Memphis, and offered him a position for an indefinite term at a $60,000 base salary with an expected minimum bonus of $25,000. He accepted by telephone two weeks later and quit his California job the same day. He then flew to Memphis to obtain housing, set up his office, meet his secretary, fill out insurance forms, and order business cards; leased an apartment; and returned to California to pack. Before he began working, the firm's managing director informed him by telephone that the firm had decided to "separate" him, and, when asked why, said he did not know. The firm reimbursed the two trips to Memphis but not the apartment deposit or any salary. The trial court granted the firm summary judgment. The Court of Appeal reversed. It held that although the analyst had not shown that the firm needed good cause to terminate him, implicit in such an employment agreement — and certainly implicit within the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, which the court described as inherent in every contract — is the understanding that an employer cannot expect a new employee to sever his former employment and move across the country only to be terminated before the ink dries on his new lease, or before he has had a chance to demonstrate his ability to satisfy the requirements of the job. The court added that the employer's conduct was governed by promissory estoppel, and adopted the reasoning of the Minnesota Supreme Court in Grouse v. Group Health Plan, Inc., a case in which an offer was revoked before the plaintiff started work: under those facts the plaintiff had a right to assume he would be given a good-faith opportunity to perform his duties to the employer's satisfaction once he was on the job. Because the firm's stated reasons for the separation were either conclusory or disputed, the court held the question could not be resolved on summary judgment.

citations.quote: The same day he accepted respondent’s offer appellant quit his California job.
On October 1 McStay informed him by telephone that respondent had decided to “separate” him before he began actively working.
Respondent reimbursed him for expenses incurred for the two trips to Memphis, but not for his apartment deposit or any salary.
There is also inherent in every contract a covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

Although appellant has not demonstrated that respondent required good cause to terminate him, implicit in such an employment agreement, and certainly implicit within the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, is the understanding that an employer cannot expect a new employee to sever his former employment and move across the country only to be terminated before the ink dries on his new lease, or before he has had a chance to demonstrate his ability to satisfy the requirements of the job.

The Minnesota Supreme Court applied promissory estoppel, concluding “that under the facts of this case the [plaintiff] had a right to assume he would be given a good faith opportunity to perform his duties to the satisfaction of [defendant] once he was on the job.” (Id., at p. 116.) We conclude the same reasoning applies here.
This is a disputed issue of fact, and cannot be resolved by summary judgment.
The summary judgment is reversed.

expectedJSON.body: Toscano v. Greene Music addresses the measure of damages when an offer is withdrawn after the applicant has resigned from other employment. The plaintiff, the general manager of a piano store, was offered a sales management position by another piano retailer to start on September 1, 2001; he resigned from his existing job on August 1 in reliance on that promise, and in mid-August the new employer withdrew the offer. He later found lower-paying work. After a bench trial on promissory estoppel, the trial court awarded him lost wages measured by what he would have earned from his former employer. On appeal, the plaintiff conceded that the weight of authority prevents an employee in his circumstances from recovering future lost wages from the prospective employer that induced him to resign — the wages of the job he never started — but argued that the law permits recovery of what he would have earned in the future from his former employer as a component of reliance damages. The Court of Appeal agreed with that framing. It noted the California Supreme Court's observation that, unless there is unjust enrichment of the promisor, promissory estoppel damages should not put the promisee in a better position than performance of the promise would have put him, but held that this limitation does not preclude recovery of some measure of future income relinquished as a result of detrimental reliance. Given the equitable underpinnings of the doctrine, the court held that a plaintiff who relinquished his job in reliance on an unfulfilled promise of employment may, on an appropriate showing, recover the lost wages he would have expected to earn from his former employer but for the defendant's promise. The court rejected the argument that the at-will nature of the former job is a strict impediment to such recovery, reasoning by analogy to the tort of interference with an at-will contract that an at-will relationship is at the will of the parties, not of outsiders, and that assessing such damages against the third-party promisor rather than against the at-will employer does not contradict or undermine California's doctrine of at-will employment.

citations.quote: Joseph Toscano sued Greene Music (Greene) for promissory estoppel stemming from Greene’s unfulfilled promise of employment, which caused Toscano to resign from an at-will employment position with his former employer.
On August 1, 2001, Toscano resigned from Fields in reliance on Michael Greene’s promise of employment.

Toscano concedes the weight of authority prevents an employee in his circumstances from recovering future lost wages from the prospective employer that induced him to resign his employment; he asserts, however, the law permits the employee to recover what he would have earned in the future from his former employer as a component of reliance damages.
‘[u]nless there is unjust enrichment of the promisor, [promissory estoppel] damages should not put the promisee in a better position than performance of the promise would have put him.’

Given the equitable underpinnings of the promissory estoppel doctrine, we hold that a plaintiff such as Toscano, who relinquished his job in reliance on an unfulfilled promise of employment, may on an appropriate showing recover the lost wages he would have expected to earn from his former employer but for the defendant’s promise.

Our holding necessarily rejects the notion that the at-will nature of Toscano’s former employment with Fields (undisputed by the parties here) is a strict impediment to recovery of future wages that Toscano would have earned at Fields had he not relied on Greene’s promise.

Unlike these cases, Toscano’s possible recovery of lost earnings from his relinquished at-will employment does not contradict or undermine California’s doctrine of at-will employment when those damages are assessed against the third party wrongdoer, not the at-will employer.

The "unjust enrichment" passage is quoted as Toscano reproduces it from Kajima/Ray Wilson and the Restatement; those sources were not separately fetched. The opinion does not address damages for relocation expenses, benefits, or emotional distress, and does not discuss mitigation, although the plaintiff's later, lower-paying jobs were netted against his former wages in the calculation the court described. The court's damages holding was expressly conditioned on proof that is not speculative, a limitation described in the next clause. expectedJSON.body: Toscano's damages holding carries an express limit. The Court of Appeal stated at the outset that lost wages from the former employer are recoverable on a promissory estoppel theory as long as they are not speculative or remote and are supported by substantial evidence, and it applied what it called the settled rule that a damage award in these circumstances must not be speculative, remote, contingent, or merely possible. Analogizing to lost-profits claims, the court held that damages for the loss of future earnings in this context are recoverable where the evidence makes reasonably certain their occurrence and extent, and described the only limitation on the plaintiff's recovery as the requirement that the fact and extent of his lost future earnings be proven with reasonable certainty. On the record before it, the court found that standard unmet as to the award of wages from September 1, 2001 (the promised start date) through the plaintiff's projected retirement in 2017. The plaintiff's accountant had calculated the difference between his former salary and his new earnings through retirement, but admitted she was unaware of any specific tenure at the former job and that he could have quit or been fired at any time; her testimony did not establish that he had a definite expectation of continued employment with the former employer for any particular period, and the plaintiff's own history of staying with employers until offered new work did not establish with reasonable certainty that an at-will employer would have kept him until the end of his career. Although the fact of damage was established, the court held the expert's conclusions as to its extent were wholly conjectural. The defendant had conceded that the plaintiff was entitled to one month of salary from the former employer — from his August 1 resignation to the promised September 1 start date. The court vacated the award of future earnings from September 1, 2001 to retirement, remanded for a new trial limited to the amount of those damages, and otherwise affirmed the judgment.

citations.quote: We hold such damages are recoverable on a promissory estoppel theory as long as they are not speculative or remote and are supported by substantial evidence, but they are not available to Toscano under the evidence in this case.

we hold a plaintiff’s lost future wages from the former at-will employer are recoverable under a promissory estoppel theory as long as they are not speculative or remote, and are supported by substantial evidence.
We apply the settled rule, however, that the court’s damage award in these circumstances must not be speculative, remote, contingent or merely possible.
The only limitation on Toscano’s recovery is that the fact and extent of his lost future earnings must be proven with reasonable certainty.
Spoon’s testimony does not establish Toscano had a definite expectation of continued employment with Fields for any particular period of time.
Although the fact of Toscano’s damage was established, Spoon’s conclusions as to the extent of Toscano’s lost employment were wholly conjectural.

Greene conceded below and concedes here that Toscano is entitled to recover damages for one month of salary from Fields, from the date of his resignation on August 1, 2001, to his start-date with Greene, September 1, 2001.

The award of future earnings calculated from September 1, 2001, to the date of Toscano’s retirement in 2017 is vacated and the matter remanded for a new trial on the issue of damages only. The judgment is otherwise affirmed.

expectedJSON.body: The promissory estoppel doctrine described in the preceding clauses does not depend on the employer's reason for withdrawing the offer. A separate body of law addresses the reason itself. Government Code section 12940 declares it an unlawful employment practice — unless based upon a bona fide occupational qualification, or except where based upon applicable security regulations established by the United States or the State of California — for an employer, because of a person's race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status, to refuse to hire or employ the person, or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment. The statute's operative verbs — refuse to hire or employ, bar, and discharge — describe employer decisions at every stage from application through separation, and the statute does not confine its coverage to persons who have already begun work. This corpus's separate information sheets on discriminatory job advertisements and applicant inquiries, on the Fair Chance Act, and on post-offer medical examinations describe other statutory limits on hiring-stage decisions.

(a) For an employer, because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status of any person, to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.
